cases.n: Poland — State Commission on Paedophilia, first and second reports (2021–2022)
cases.victims_note: 188 girls and 173 boys in 345 cases and 245 court proceedings analysed
cases.who: Polish justice system; Catholic clergy (almost 30% of perpetrators in the cases studied)
cases.d: Poland's State Commission on Paedophilia, set up by the government after a 2020 documentary on abuse and alleged cover-ups in the Catholic Church, published its first report on 29 July 2021. It analysed 345 cases and 245 court proceedings involving 188 girls and 173 boys, most aged 11 to 15. Almost 30% of perpetrators were clergy and 35% were relatives. In half the cases no one had noticed signs of abuse. The commission sent 137 notifications to prosecutors and made 22 recommendations, including ending the statute of limitations for child sexual abuse. Its second report, published on 2 August 2022, covered 513 cases; among abusers who were not relatives, clergy were the largest professional group (57 cases, about 47%).
cases.cite: Państwowa Komisja do spraw przeciwdziałania wykorzystaniu seksualnemu małoletnich poniżej lat 15, first report, July 2021 (Notes from Poland, 29 July 2021); second report, 2 August 2022 (Prawo.pl)

cases.n: Poland — Diocese of Sosnowiec independent commission (2026)
cases.victims_note: at least 50 children; 96% under 15
cases.who: Catholic Diocese of Sosnowiec
cases.cover: Bishops were repeatedly alerted, including by reliable sources, but often took no action; where they acted, they usually moved the priest to another parish.
cases.d: The independent commission 'Wyjaśnienie i Naprawa', set up in October 2024 and chaired by journalist Tomasz Krzyżak, presented its findings on 12 February 2026 after reviewing diocesan files from 1992 to January 2025. It found at least 50 children harmed and 29 people accused, 23 of them diocesan clergy; 19 of the 23 priests were confirmed offenders in church or state proceedings. Bishops were repeatedly warned but often did nothing, and accused priests were usually transferred. The commission reported eight people to prosecutors. It was the first such diocesan commission report in Poland.
cases.cite: Commission 'Wyjaśnienie i Naprawa', report on the Diocese of Sosnowiec, 12 February 2026 (Notes from Poland, 13 February 2026)

cases.n: Spain — Cremades & Calvo-Sotelo audit for the Episcopal Conference (2023)
cases.victims_note: at least 2,056 minors, counted from complaints and lawsuits; the Episcopal Conference said the real number is higher
cases.who: Spanish Episcopal Conference; Catholic clergy, religious and lay church staff
cases.d: The Spanish Episcopal Conference hired the law firm Cremades & Calvo-Sotelo in February 2022 to audit abuse by clergy, teachers and other church staff. The church announced its findings on 21 December 2023: at least 2,056 minor victims and 1,383 complaints. The figure is far below the Ombudsman's survey-based estimate published two months earlier, and the bishops said the true number was obviously higher.
cases.cite: Cremades & Calvo-Sotelo audit for the Conferencia Episcopal Española, December 2023 (The Local Spain / AFP, 21 December 2023)

cases.n: Belgium — Chamber special committee on sexual abuse in the Church (Lalieux, 2011)
cases.who: Catholic Church in Belgium; Belgian justice system
cases.d: After the June 2010 police raids that ended the Adriaenssens commission, the Belgian Chamber set up a special committee on the handling of sexual abuse in relationships of authority, especially within the Church, chaired by Karine Lalieux. Its report, approved unanimously on 30 March 2011, found abuse in every sector of the church and across the country, especially in Catholic boarding schools, with families reporting at least 13 suicides. It recommended an independent arbitration body for compensation and extending the limitation period from 10 to 15 years after a victim turns 18. The arbitration centre and its compensation scheme followed in 2012.
cases.cite: Chambre des représentants, Commission spéciale relative au traitement d'abus sexuels et de faits de pédophilie dans une relation d'autorité, report adopted 30 March 2011 (AP via Deseret News, 30 March 2011)

cases.n: France — CIIVISE final report on sexual violence against children (2023)
cases.victims_note: estimate of children who are victims of sexual violence each year in France
cases.who: French justice, health and child-protection systems; families and institutions
cases.d: The Independent Commission on Incest and Sexual Violence against Children (CIIVISE), created by the government on 11 March 2021 and chaired by juvenile judge Édouard Durand, delivered its final report on 20 November 2023 with 82 recommendations. It estimated that 160,000 children suffer sexual violence each year in France. It found that victims wait 10 to 13 years on average for specialised care and that only 5% of reports come from doctors. The commission's work covers abuse in families and in institutions, and the failures of courts, police and health services to act.
cases.cite: CIIVISE, 'Violences sexuelles faites aux enfants : on vous croit', 20 November 2023 (Fondation Raja summary, 8 December 2023)

cases.n: France — National Assembly inquiry into failings of sports federations (2024)
cases.victims_note: Signal-sports cell: 1,800+ reports concerning 1,200+ people by Nov 2023; 8 in 10 victims were minors
cases.who: French sports federations (incl. judo, ice sports, football), sports ministry
cases.cover: Inspectorate inquiries into judo and ice sports found an 'omerta at every level, up to the highest levels of the state'; the ministry did not provide the Signal-sports data to the commission.
cases.d: A National Assembly commission of inquiry chaired by Béatrice Bellamy, with Sabrina Sebaihi as rapporteur, worked from July 2023 and presented its report in January 2024 after 92 hearings. It found that by November 2023 the ministry's Signal-sports cell had handled over 1,800 reports involving more than 1,200 people, with eight in ten victims minors at the time. Background checks on volunteers, required since 2006, only began working in 2021, and 42 federations were behind. The report described a culture of silence and concealment in federations and in the state.
cases.cite: Assemblée nationale, Commission d'enquête relative à l'identification des défaillances de fonctionnement au sein des fédérations françaises de sport, report no. 2012, press kit 23 January 2024

cases.n: France — Senate mission on sexual offences against minors by people working with children (2019)
cases.who: Catholic Church in France, sports federations, schools, holiday camps, centres for disabled children
cases.d: A French Senate information mission, with Marie Mercier and Michelle Meunier as rapporteurs, presented its report on 29 May 2019 after hearing more than 60 people. It found a 'systemic problem' in the Catholic Church, citing the sacred status of priests, fear of scandal and a culture of secrecy, and flagged sports federations and centres for disabled children as high-risk. It made 38 recommendations, including checking the sex-offender register before every hire to work with minors. A request for a full Senate commission of inquiry into the Church was refused.
cases.cite: Sénat, mission commune d'information sur la répression des infractions sexuelles sur mineurs, report no. 529, 28 May 2019 (Public Sénat, 29 May 2019)

cases.n: Netherlands — De Vries Commission on sexual abuse in organised sport (2017)
cases.victims_note: 686 cases reported to the sport confidential line 2001–2017, 60% under 16; survey: about 12% of athletes had such experiences as children
cases.who: Dutch sports clubs and federations; NOC*NSF
cases.d: The Dutch Olympic Committee NOC*NSF set up a commission led by former minister Klaas de Vries in May 2017; it reported on 12 December 2017. A survey found about 12% of athletes had experienced sexually transgressive behaviour as children and about 4% sexual assault or rape. The commission analysed 686 cases reported between 2001 and 2017, in which 60% of victims were under 16 and 70% of perpetrators were coaches or supervisors, and received 103 new reports. It recommended a reporting duty for sports boards.
cases.cite: Commissie De Vries, 'Onderzoek naar seksuele intimidatie en misbruik in de sport', December 2017 (NOS, 12 December 2017)

cases.n: Germany — Conference of Religious Superiors (DOK) survey of abuse in Catholic orders (2020)
cases.victims_note: at least 1,412 children, adolescents or wards (80% male); DOK says unreported cases cannot be counted
cases.who: Catholic religious orders in Germany (100 of 291 responding orders)
cases.d: The German Conference of Catholic Religious Superiors (DOK) surveyed 392 orders in 2019 and published the results on 26 August 2020. The 291 orders that answered, covering 88% of members, recorded accusations against at least 654 members and 58 other staff, from at least 1,412 children, adolescents or wards. Accusations were recorded in 53 of 77 male orders and 47 of 214 female orders. About 80% of the accused had died. Religious orders had been left out of the 2018 MHG study.
cases.cite: Deutsche Ordensobernkonferenz, survey results, 26 August 2020 (America magazine / CNS, 26 August 2020)

cases.n: Germany — Independent Commission case study on abuse in sport (2022)
cases.who: German sports clubs and federations (West and East Germany)
cases.d: Germany's federal Independent Commission for the Investigation of Child Sexual Abuse (UKASK) published a case study on sport on 27 September 2022, based on 72 reports from victims and witnesses and three personal accounts. Most abuse happened in competitive club sport, by male coaches or teachers in positions of power, and two-thirds of victims were abused repeatedly. Nearly a fifth of reports concerned sport in the GDR. Very few cases had been uncovered; victims who spoke up were often disbelieved or their accounts concealed.
cases.cite: Unabhängige Kommission zur Aufarbeitung sexuellen Kindesmissbrauchs, 'Sexualisierte Gewalt und sexueller Kindesmissbrauch im Kontext des Sports', 27 September 2022 (epd via evangelisch.de)

cases.n: Germany — Independent Commission case study on child sexual abuse in the GDR (2019)
cases.victims_note: based on accounts of about 100 people abused as children in the GDR
cases.who: GDR children's homes and Jugendwerkhöfe (youth work homes); families
cases.d: The federal Independent Commission for the Investigation of Child Sexual Abuse presented a case study on the GDR on 6 March 2019, based on accounts from about 100 people abused as children. Boys were more often abused in state homes, including the Jugendwerkhöfe, and girls more often in their families. The accounts included children being organised and sold for sexual services. The study found abuse in the GDR was widespread and remained taboo longer than in West Germany.
cases.cite: Unabhängige Kommission zur Aufarbeitung sexuellen Kindesmissbrauchs, Fallstudie DDR, 6 March 2019 (Deutsches Ärzteblatt, 6 March 2019)

cases.n: Germany — Federal Independent Commissioner (Bergmann) final report (2011)
cases.victims_note: about 13,000 letters and 2,000 calls from victims and relatives
cases.who: Churches, schools, sports clubs, homes and families in Germany
cases.d: After the 2010 revelations at Canisius-Kolleg and other schools, the federal government appointed former minister Christine Bergmann as Independent Commissioner. Her final report, presented on 24 May 2011 to the Round Table on Child Sexual Abuse, drew on about 13,000 letters and 2,000 phone calls from victims and relatives about abuse in churches, schools, sports clubs and families. It recommended that institutions where abuse occurred pay compensation at the level courts would award, coverage of therapy costs, and a permanent independent body. This led to the permanent federal commissioner's office and, in 2016, the Independent Commission.
cases.cite: Abschlussbericht der Unabhängigen Beauftragten zur Aufarbeitung des sexuellen Kindesmissbrauchs, 24 May 2011 (epd via evangelisch.de)

cases.n: Germany — SOS-Kinderdorf independent commission report (2024)
cases.victims_note: 226 known cases of boundary violations (physical, psychological and sexual), incl. rapes in individual cases
cases.who: SOS-Kinderdorf e.V. (Germany) — children's villages and group homes
cases.d: An independent commission appointed by SOS-Kinderdorf e.V. investigated from 2021 and presented its report in Munich on 2 October 2024. It recorded 226 known cases of boundary violations since the organisation's founding in 1955, 189 from its internal reporting office and 37 from a 2023 newspaper appeal, including sexual assaults and in some cases rape. About half were committed by staff such as house parents and about 20% by other young people in care. The commission said the closed nature of SOS family units was a risk and that more cases are likely unrecorded.
cases.cite: Unabhängige Kommission SOS-Kinderdorf, Abschlussbericht, 2 October 2024 (epd via evangelisch.de)

cases.n: Germany — Nordelbian Lutheran Church expert commission (Ahrensburg, 2014)
cases.who: Former Nordelbian Evangelical Lutheran Church (now Nordkirche)
cases.cover: Cases became public in 2010; the Ahrensburg pastor faced no criminal case because the offences were time-barred; Hamburg bishop Maria Jepsen resigned over the church's handling.
cases.d: An independent commission of lawyers and social scientists published its final report in October 2014 on abuse in the former Nordelbian Lutheran Church. It examined 14 pastors against whom the church opened 16 disciplinary proceedings between 1993 and 2012, for acts from 1973 to 2011 against children, adolescents and adults in pastoral care. The case that started it was a pastor in Ahrensburg who abused at least a dozen children over more than 20 years. Bishop Kirsten Fehrs said the church as an institution had become guilty.
cases.cite: Unabhängige Expertenkommission, report on sexual abuse in the Nordelbian Church, October 2014 (epd via evangelisch.de, 15 October 2014)

cases.n: Germany — Ettal Benedictine abbey boarding school, IPP study (2013)
cases.who: Benedictine Abbey of Ettal and its boarding school
cases.d: After abuse at the Ettal abbey school became public in 2010 and police searched the monastery, the abbey commissioned the Munich Institute for Practice Research (IPP, Heiner Keupp and Florian Straus). Its study, presented on 7 March 2013 from 41 interviews and abbey records, found physical, psychological and sexualised violence over at least three decades, mostly from the 1960s to the 1980s. It described a 'culture of enabling' rather than a planned system. An earlier special investigator's report appeared in 2010–2011.
cases.cite: IPP München (Keupp, Straus et al.), study on violence at Ettal boarding school, 7 March 2013 (epd via evangelisch.de)

cases.n: Germany — Bund der Pfadfinderinnen und Pfadfinder (BdP) study (2024)
cases.victims_note: 103 identified, 123 incl. cases that could not be dated or assigned
cases.who: Bund der Pfadfinderinnen und Pfadfinder (non-denominational scout association)
cases.d: The BdP commissioned IPP Munich and the Dissens institute to study sexualised violence in the association from its founding in 1976 to 2006. Presented on 29 February 2024, the study identified 103 victims (123 including cases that could not be dated or assigned) and 36 accused (50 with the same additions). It found two main perpetrator types, older adult leaders and adolescents who used leadership roles, and said weak oversight, group loyalty and the handling of rumours made disclosure harder.
cases.cite: IPP München / Dissens, study for the Bund der Pfadfinderinnen und Pfadfinder, 29 February 2024 (IPP press release)

cases.n: Germany — Catholic scouts (DPSG) study on sexualised and spiritual violence (2026)
cases.victims_note: no count given; study not representative; victims mainly girls and young women
cases.who: Deutsche Pfadfinder*innenschaft Sankt Georg (DPSG), Catholic scout association
cases.d: Researchers from the universities of Marburg and Gießen, led by Sabine Maschke and Ludwig Stecher, studied sexualised and spiritual violence in the Catholic scout association DPSG from 1929 to 2022 and presented the results in Cologne on 5 February 2026. They found sexualised violence was a widespread structural problem, especially on camps and trips, mostly by male leaders against underage girls, and that the association had looked away and played incidents down. Over 90% of the accused were male. The DPSG accepted institutional responsibility.
cases.cite: Universities of Marburg and Gießen, study for the DPSG, 5 February 2026 (JLU Gießen press release; epd)

cases.n: Germany — Archdiocese of Cologne, Gercke report (2021)
cases.victims_note: more than half under 14
cases.who: Catholic Archdiocese of Cologne
cases.cover: The report counted 75 breaches of duty by eight senior archdiocesan officials; an earlier report by Westpfahl Spilker Wastl was withheld by the archdiocese.
cases.d: Criminal lawyer Björn Gercke, mandated by the archdiocese, presented an 800-page report on 18 March 2021 covering 1975 to 2018. It found 314 victims, more than half under 14, and 202 accused clergy and lay staff. It counted 75 breaches of duty by eight senior officials, among them the later Archbishop of Hamburg Stefan Heße, while clearing Cardinal Rainer Maria Woelki of breach of duty. Woelki had withheld an earlier report by another law firm, which caused a long crisis in the archdiocese.
cases.cite: Gercke Wollschläger, 'Pflichtverletzungen von Diözesanverantwortlichen im Erzbistum Köln …', 18 March 2021 (The Local / AFP; KNA via Vatican News)

cases.n: Germany — Diocese of Münster, University of Münster study (2022)
cases.victims_note: at least 610 minors; authors estimate the real number 8 to 10 times higher
cases.who: Catholic Diocese of Münster
cases.cover: The study found a 'massive leadership failure' under the bishops from 1947 to 2008; most accused priests were transferred rather than restricted.
cases.d: Historians at the University of Münster, including Thomas Großbölting, published a study of the diocese on 13 June 2022 after about two and a half years of research. It found at least 610 minors abused by 196 clerics between 1945 and 2020, about 4% of the diocese's priests in that period, and estimated the real number of victims at 8 to 10 times higher. Bishops and diocesan leaders were often fully informed, covered up cases or intervened only superficially, and usually transferred accused priests.
cases.cite: University of Münster, study on sexual abuse of minors by clergy in the Diocese of Münster 1945–2020, 13 June 2022 (AP via Religion News Service)

cases.n: Germany — Archdiocese of Freiburg commission report (2023)
cases.victims_note: more than 540 people assumed affected; earlier count at least 442
cases.who: Catholic Archdiocese of Freiburg
cases.cover: The report found that Archbishop Robert Zollitsch (2003–2013) disregarded church law, reported no cases to Rome although required from 2002, and that files were manipulated; Archbishop Oskar Saier moved offenders without telling parishes.
cases.d: The archdiocese's independent reappraisal commission presented a roughly 600-page report on 18 April 2023, examining 24 cases in depth from 1945 onward. The commission chair said more than 540 people were assumed to have been victims of more than 250 clerics. It found that former archbishop Robert Zollitsch, who also chaired the German Bishops' Conference from 2008 to 2014, deliberately concealed cases and ignored canon law, and that his predecessor Oskar Saier transferred offenders without informing parishes.
cases.cite: Unabhängige Aufarbeitungskommission / AG Aktenanalyse, Erzdiözese Freiburg, report of 18 April 2023 (Vatican News; KNA/Pillar via BishopAccountability)

cases.n: Germany — Diocese of Mainz, EVV study (2023)
cases.victims_note: 657 possible victims identified, 401 after review
cases.who: Catholic Diocese of Mainz
cases.cover: The study said that under Bishops Stohr, Volk and Cardinal Karl Lehmann protecting offenders and the Church came before victims; it described Lehmann's early years (1983–2001) as 'deflecting and dissembling'.
cases.d: The study 'Erfahren. Verstehen. Vorsorgen.' by lawyer Ulrich Weber, commissioned by the diocese in 2019, was released on 3 March 2023. It identified 657 possible victims and 392 suspects for 1945 to 2019, of whom 401 victims and 181 accused remained after review. It found that Cardinal Karl Lehmann, bishop from 1983 to 2016 and long-time head of the German Bishops' Conference, never met his own public standard for handling abuse. Bishop Peter Kohlgraf said protecting offenders and the Church had mattered more to his predecessors than the victims.
cases.cite: Ulrich Weber and Johannes Baumeister, 'Erfahren. Verstehen. Vorsorgen.' (EVV), Diocese of Mainz, 3 March 2023 (AP via BishopAccountability)

cases.n: Germany — Diocese of Aachen, Westpfahl Spilker Wastl report (2020)
cases.victims_note: at least 175 cases with indications of abuse of children and adolescents, most aged 8 to 14
cases.who: Catholic Diocese of Aachen
cases.cover: The report assigned personal responsibility to former Bishop Heinrich Mussinghoff and his vicar general Manfred von Holtum.
cases.d: The Munich law firm Westpfahl Spilker Wastl, commissioned by the diocese, presented its report on 12 November 2020 after reviewing files from 1965 to 2019. It found at least 175 cases with indications of sexual abuse of children and adolescents by 81 clerics (79 priests and two deacons), most victims aged 8 to 14. It assigned personal responsibility to former bishop Heinrich Mussinghoff and his vicar general. It was the first of the German diocesan legal reports to be published in full.
cases.cite: Westpfahl Spilker Wastl, Gutachten for the Diocese of Aachen, 12 November 2020 (epd via evangelisch.de)

cases.n: Germany — Diocese of Essen, IPP study (2023)
cases.who: Catholic Diocese of Essen
cases.cover: Accused priests were often moved to other posts, sometimes in other dioceses; parishes were not informed, and until 2010 the diocese made no effort to support victims.
cases.d: The Munich IPP institute, with the Berlin institute Dissens, published its study of the diocese's 65 years on 14 February 2023. It found 226 people who reported abuse and 190 accused clergy in the records, with most offences in the 1950s to 1970s. Accused priests were often reassigned, sometimes to other dioceses, without parishes being told, and until 2010 the diocese did nothing to support victims. Bishop Franz-Josef Overbeck acknowledged the failures; about 1.9 million euros had been paid to victims.
cases.cite: IPP München / Dissens (Helga Dill et al.), study of sexualised violence in the Diocese of Essen, 14 February 2023 (epd via evangelisch.de)

cases.n: Germany — Archdiocese of Berlin, Redeker Sellner Dahs report (2021)
cases.victims_note: at least 121 known victims
cases.who: Catholic Archdiocese of Berlin
cases.d: The law firm Redeker Sellner Dahs, commissioned by the Archbishop of Berlin, presented its report in part on 29 January 2021, covering 1946 to 2019. It found at least 61 clergy involved in abuse of minors and 121 known victims. A part on the responsibility of named officials was kept back and later reviewed by another firm and presented at the end of June 2021.
cases.cite: Redeker Sellner Dahs, Gutachten for the Archdiocese of Berlin, 29 January 2021 (KNA via Vatican News; German Bishops' Conference overview, 13 December 2022)

cases.n: Germany — Diocese of Trier independent commission (2022 onward)
cases.victims_note: identified so far in the August 2022 interim report
cases.who: Catholic Diocese of Trier
cases.cover: Bishop Bernhard Stein (1967–1980) is accused of covering up cases; the commission's later reports examine his tenure and the terms of Reinhard Marx (bishop 2002–2008) and Georg Bätzing (vicar general 2012–2016).
cases.d: The diocese's independent commission, launched in June 2021 with Gerhard Robbers as spokesman, released its interim report in August 2022 covering 1946 to 2021. It had identified 513 victims and 195 perpetrators so far. Later commission studies examined the terms of bishops Bernhard Stein (2022) and Hermann Josef Spital (2024).
cases.cite: Unabhängige Kommission zur Aufarbeitung des sexuellen Missbrauchs im Bistum Trier, interim report, August 2022 (The Pillar via BishopAccountability, 13 October 2022)

cases.n: Germany — Diocese of Osnabrück, University of Osnabrück study (2022–2024)
cases.who: Catholic Diocese of Osnabrück
cases.cover: The interim report found Bishop Franz-Josef Bode repeatedly left accused priests in office and gave some roles, including youth ministry, that enabled further offences; Bode resigned in March 2023.
cases.d: Historians and lawyers at the University of Osnabrück, commissioned by the diocese, presented a roughly 600-page interim report on 20 September 2022 on sexual violence by clergy since 1945; the final report followed in 2024. The interim report criticised the handling of allegations under Bishop Franz-Josef Bode (from 1995) and his predecessors, finding he repeatedly left accused priests in office and assigned some to posts that enabled further abuse. Bode accepted responsibility and resigned in 2023.
cases.cite: University of Osnabrück (Schulte-Nölke, Westphal et al.), interim report for the Diocese of Osnabrück, 20 September 2022 (The Pillar via BishopAccountability)

cases.n: Austria — Kremsmünster Abbey school abuse, diocesan commission and IPP study
cases.victims_note: 45 people reported abuse at the Stiftsgymnasium to the Diocese of Linz commission within a year (sexual, physical or psychological)
cases.who: Benedictine Abbey of Kremsmünster and its Stiftsgymnasium
cases.d: Within a year of reports in March 2010, 45 former pupils told the Diocese of Linz commission of abuse at the Kremsmünster abbey school from the 1970s to the 1990s; three priests were accused of sexual abuse and eight people of physical or psychological abuse. In 2013 an Austrian court convicted the former school director, a monk, in 24 cases and sentenced him to 12 years. By February 2013 the abbey had paid 700,000 euros to victims, and in March 2013 it commissioned IPP Munich to study the background; that study appeared in 2016.
cases.cite: German Wikipedia, 'Sexueller Missbrauch in der römisch-katholischen Kirche in Österreich' (Kremsmünster section); English Wikipedia, 'Catholic Church sexual abuse cases by country' (Austria)

cases.n: Italy — Il Forteto community, Tuscany: abuse of children placed by courts
cases.who: Il Forteto agricultural cooperative and community; Tuscany Region, juvenile court and local authorities that placed and accredited it
cases.cover: The founder already had a final conviction in 1985, yet courts and social services kept placing children there; parliament's 2024 commission is to establish why authorities kept accrediting the community after court rulings on sexual abuse and mistreatment.
cases.d: Il Forteto, a cooperative and community in the Mugello near Florence, received children placed by juvenile courts and social services for decades. Its founder, Rodolfo Fiesoli, was definitively sentenced to 14 years and 10 months for abuse, although an earlier conviction had become final in 1985 and placements continued. Two Tuscan regional council inquiry commissions examined the case; a parliamentary commission set up by law in 2019 did not approve a final report, and a new bicameral commission of inquiry was created by Law 47 of 25 March 2024 and installed in August 2024.
cases.cite: Camera dei deputati, Law 47/2024 on the parliamentary commission of inquiry on Il Forteto (temi.camera.it); La Nazione, 1 August 2024

cases.n: Belgium (Flanders) — expert panel and Ethiopia investigation on intercountry adoption malpractice
cases.victims_note: 936 children adopted from Ethiopia to Flanders 1996–2017; 12 families' files examined
cases.who: Flemish adoption services; intermediaries in Ethiopia and other countries of origin
cases.d: After reports of malpractice in adoptions from Ethiopia in 2019, the Flemish government appointed an independent expert panel on intercountry adoption, which delivered its findings in 2021 (final report dated February 2023), and funded the Flemish Centre for Adoption to examine Ethiopian adoptions from 1997 to 2015. That investigation found that in the worst cases children had not been given up voluntarily by their birth parents and that files differed from the real story. The panel's work led to screening of all countries of origin, after which Flanders stopped adoptions from Vietnam, Gambia, Haiti and Morocco.
cases.cite: Flemish expert panel on intercountry adoption (2021–2023); Vlaams Centrum voor Adoptie, Ethiopia investigation (Brussels Times, 23 November 2023); Belga News Agency
